lessons.title: Organisational Structures
lessons.description: Tall versus flat, span of control, delegation and centralised versus decentralised decision-making.
lessons.content_html:
Every business, from a two-person coffee van to a supermarket chain, needs a way of showing who reports to whom. That is the job of the organisational structure. It sets out job roles, responsibilities and lines of communication so that decisions flow from managers to staff and work gets done in the right order.

Tall and Flat Structures

A tall structure has many layers of management. Think of an NHS hospital trust: a chief executive sits above directors, who sit above senior managers, ward managers and then clinical staff. Each manager has only a few people reporting directly to them, which means tight supervision and clear career ladders — but also slow decisions, because a message has to climb many rungs.

A flat structure has few layers. A tech start-up of twenty people might have a founder, one team of engineers and one team of marketers — that’s it. Decisions are quick, staff feel trusted, and costs are lower because there are fewer managers to pay. The trade-off is that each manager supervises a lot of people, so they cannot give much individual attention.

Key Fact

Tall structures give tight supervision and clear promotion paths but slow communication. Flat structures give fast decisions and lower management costs but wider spans of control.

Span of Control and Chain of Command

The span of control is the number of people a single manager oversees. A narrow span (three or four staff) allows close mentoring; a wide span (fifteen or more) demands that workers manage themselves. The chain of command is the route an instruction travels from the top of the business to the bottom. A long chain means careful control; a short chain means fewer people reword the message, so it arrives clearly.

Delayering is the deliberate removal of layers of management. After the 2008 financial crisis, UK banks such as Lloyds and Barclays cut thousands of middle-management roles. The aim was to reduce wage costs, speed up decisions and give branch staff more responsibility. The risk is that remaining managers end up overloaded and staff morale drops as colleagues are made redundant.

Delegation

Delegation is when a manager hands a task, and the authority to complete it, to an employee further down the chain. A supermarket duty manager might delegate a promotional display to a supervisor. Good delegation motivates staff by showing trust, develops skills and frees managers for bigger decisions. Poor delegation — giving someone a task they are not trained for or refusing to let them decide — can cause mistakes and resentment.

Centralised and Decentralised Decisions

In a centralised business, head office makes the big calls. McDonald’s UK decides the menu, prices and suppliers centrally so that a burger tastes the same in Carlisle as it does in Cardiff. In a decentralised business, power is pushed down to local managers. A chain of independent garden centres might let each manager choose their own plant supplier to suit local demand.

A new start-up usually has a flat, decentralised structure because the team is small and speed matters. As the business grows it often adds layers to keep control — Deliveroo was famously flat when it launched in 2013 but added regional management as it expanded. Mature, safety-critical organisations such as NHS trusts and the Royal Navy stay tall because clear lines of responsibility matter more than speed. Neither shape is ‘better’ — the right answer depends on size, sector and how much local variation the business wants.

Communication and Job Roles

Structure shapes communication. In a tall organisation, instructions travel vertically and may be distorted as each layer reinterprets the message — think of a message passed from an NHS trust board down through directors, senior nurses and ward leaders before it reaches a junior nurse. In a flat one, staff can speak directly to the person making the decision, which tends to raise morale and speeds up a fix. Every structure also sets out job roles — the directors set strategy, managers plan, supervisors organise and operatives carry out the work. When roles overlap or are missing, work falls through the gaps, so the organisation chart and job descriptions must be kept up to date.

Communication can be vertical (up or down the chain), horizontal (between colleagues at the same level) or diagonal (across departments). A wide span of control usually pushes a business towards horizontal communication, because managers cannot brief every worker in person. Good organisational structure therefore sets up channels as well as layers — team meetings, internal messaging and shared dashboards all help decisions reach the right people quickly.

Appropriateness — No One-Size-Fits-All

There is no perfect structure. A two-person coffee van needs no chart on a wall, just a clear split of tasks. A national retailer needs a tall, partly centralised structure so that shop staff across hundreds of sites all follow the same standards. The appropriate structure depends on the size of the business, the sector it competes in, the experience of staff and how quickly the market changes. Fast-moving sectors like fashion and tech tend towards flatter, decentralised shapes so they can respond to customers; regulated sectors like banking and healthcare tend to stay taller so risks can be managed tightly.

Key Fact

Span of control = how many staff a manager supervises. Chain of command = how far an instruction travels. Delayering = cutting management layers. Delegation = passing authority down.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to analyse or evaluate a structure, do not just describe it — link the choice to the business in the case study. A small start-up with ten staff should not be given the same answer as a national supermarket. Use the command word: ‘Explain’ needs a ‘because’ clause, ‘Analyse’ needs a chain of reasoning (‘which leads to… which means…’) and ‘Evaluate’ needs a judgement that weighs the trade-offs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tall structures suit large, control-focused businesses like NHS trusts; flat structures suit start-ups that need quick decisions.
  • Span of control, chain of command, delayering and delegation all describe how authority and instructions move through a business.
  • Centralised businesses keep control at head office for consistency; decentralised businesses push decisions down for local flexibility.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a flat organisational structure?
A) Many layers of management and narrow spans of control
B) Few layers of management and wide spans of control
C) All decisions taken at head office
D) No chain of command at all
practice_questions.marks:
B) Few layers of management and wide spans of control [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct answer selected.
Emerging: Incorrect answer.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘span of control’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2 marks): Clear definition — the number of employees a manager is directly responsible for / directly supervises.
Secure (1 mark): Basic idea of ‘how many people a manager looks after’ without precise wording.
Emerging (0 marks): Vague or incorrect reference (e.g. ‘how the business is controlled’).

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit for a small technology start-up of having a flat organisational structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Clear benefit identified (e.g. fast decision-making) + explanation with a ‘because’ clause (fewer layers means instructions travel quickly) + linked to a start-up context (important when competing against larger rivals).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but not applied to a start-up.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named without explanation.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A bank has 5 senior managers, each responsible for 8 branch managers. After delayering, 2 senior manager posts are removed and their branches are shared equally among the remaining 3. Calculate the new average span of control for the 3 remaining senior managers. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Total branch managers = 5 × 8 = 40. New span = 40 ÷ 3 = 13.33 (accept 13.3 or 13).
Secure (2 marks): Correct total (40) found but arithmetic slip in the division.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working shown (e.g. spotted 40 branch managers) but no final answer.
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a large supermarket chain of moving from a centralised to a decentralised structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. local managers can respond to local tastes (ethnic food ranges, seasonal stock) which raises sales and customer loyalty; however, brand consistency may weaken, because each store decides differently, which could confuse shoppers.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains. Some application to a supermarket.
Developing (1–2 marks): Relevant points but mostly a list, little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: A growing e-commerce business currently has a tall structure with 6 layers of management. The CEO is considering delayering to 3 layers. Justify whether or not the CEO should delayer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9 marks): Two developed reasons supporting the chosen option (one fully explained) — e.g. faster communication in online markets, lower wage costs. Weighed against at least one counter-argument (redundancies harm morale; overloaded remaining managers). Clear, supported judgement.
Secure (4–6 marks): Some development of both sides. Judgement present but brief.
Developing (1–3 marks): Mainly a list of pros and cons. Limited or no judgement.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

lessons.title: Recruitment & Selection
lessons.description: Internal vs external recruitment, selection stages, and the contract types businesses use.
lessons.content_html:
When a business grows, loses a worker or launches a new product, it needs to fill a job. Recruitment and selection are the linked processes of finding applicants and picking the best one. Get it right and productivity, quality and customer service all rise; get it wrong and the business spends money training someone who soon leaves.

Internal vs External Recruitment

Internal recruitment means filling the vacancy from existing staff — by promotion, transfer or re-deployment. John Lewis, the employee-owned department store, often promotes partners from the shop floor into management roles. Internal recruits already know the company’s culture, so induction is shorter and cheaper, and promoting from within motivates the rest of the team.

External recruitment means hiring from outside — through job adverts, recruitment agencies, social media or universities. Fresh applicants bring new ideas and skills. A tech firm switching to AI might need engineers it cannot grow internally. The downside is cost: advertising fees, longer induction and the risk the new hire doesn’t fit.

Key Fact

Internal recruitment is faster, cheaper and motivates staff — but creates another vacancy and limits fresh ideas. External recruitment widens the talent pool but costs more and takes longer.

The Selection Process

Selection starts with a job analysis — the business works out exactly what the role involves. This feeds into a job description (what the post-holder will do) and a person specification (the skills and qualities the ideal candidate needs). The vacancy is then advertised, CVs are screened and the best candidates invited to interview.

Interviews are the most common selection method, but they can be unreliable — good talkers may not be good workers. Many businesses now use extra methods: skills tests (a coding challenge at Dyson), presentations (marketing roles at Unilever), group tasks (graduate schemes at PwC) and assessment centres that combine several tests over a day. References from previous employers are usually the final step before a job offer.

Why Good Recruitment Matters

An effective recruitment process raises productivity because skilled staff complete more tasks to a higher standard. It improves quality and customer service, because employees who match the role make fewer mistakes. It also supports staff retention — when new hires fit the role, they stay longer, cutting the cost of re-recruiting.

Contracts of Employment

Once someone is hired, their working terms are set out in a contract of employment. UK law requires one to be issued on or before an employee’s first day.

  • A full-time contract usually means 35–40 hours a week. It gives the employer a committed worker and the employee a stable income and holiday pay — used for most core roles at Premier League clubs’ academies and at retailers like M&S.
  • A part-time contract covers fewer hours — perhaps 16 a week. It helps parents, students and carers. For the business, part-time contracts add flexibility and lower fixed wage costs.
  • A job share lets two employees split one full-time role. The business keeps a full-time post filled but gets twice the range of skills.
  • A zero-hour contract guarantees no set hours. Workers are called in as needed — common in hospitality and retail. It gives businesses maximum flexibility and keeps costs down when demand is quiet, but workers have no guaranteed income and little security.

Full-time contracts help a business build loyal, experienced teams and spread training costs over many years of service. Employees get job security, a clear career path and a predictable wage. Part-time contracts help businesses match staffing to demand — a café can run three staff at lunchtime and one mid-afternoon — and let businesses tap into workers who cannot commit to full hours, such as parents during school hours, widening the talent pool.

Costs of Getting It Wrong

Recruitment is expensive. Estimates from the CIPD (the UK’s HR professional body) put the cost of replacing an average employee at a few thousand pounds once advert fees, manager time, lost output during the vacancy and induction training are added up. For skilled roles the figure is far higher. That is why an ‘effective’ recruitment and selection process matters — it cuts wasted spend and keeps productivity steady while the vacancy is filled. A sloppy process that picks the wrong person means repeating the whole cycle a few months later.

Effective recruitment also feeds into the wider business. A Premier League academy that recruits the right coaches develops better young players and protects the first-team pipeline. A supermarket that hires well at checkout reduces queues, raises customer service ratings and lifts repeat visits. In short, recruitment is not just a HR chore — it is a competitive advantage.

Key Fact

Full-time, part-time, job share and zero-hour are the four main contract types. Each trades off flexibility for the business against security for the employee.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Justify a Decision’ questions on recruitment, pick one option clearly and build two developed reasons — don’t sit on the fence. For Calculate questions involving recruitment costs (e.g. cost per hire), show every step of your working so you can still earn method marks if the final number is wrong. Always include units (£ or %).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal recruitment is quick and motivating; external recruitment brings fresh skills but costs more.
  • Selection uses job analysis, job description, person specification, advert, shortlist, interview and references.
  • Full-time, part-time, job share and zero-hour contracts balance business flexibility against employee security.

lessons.title: Motivation
lessons.description: Financial and non-financial motivation, and how it drives retention and productivity.
lessons.content_html:
Motivation is what makes a worker turn up on time, focus for the full shift and care about the outcome. A demotivated team produces less, makes more mistakes and quits faster. A motivated team is why a Premier League academy coach, a call-centre team leader or an Amazon warehouse manager will all tell you the same thing — how you treat people matters as much as what you pay them.

Why Motivation Matters

A motivated workforce raises productivity because engaged employees work harder and smarter. It also raises staff retention: workers who feel valued stay, cutting recruitment and training costs. Retention matters most in skilled roles — losing a senior engineer or a trained chef is expensive and slows the business down. High motivation also improves product quality and customer service, as workers take pride in their output.

Key Fact

A motivated workforce gives a business higher productivity, better staff retention, improved quality and stronger customer service — all of which cut costs and raise profits.

Financial Methods of Motivation

Financial methods use money to motivate. The main forms of payment are:

  • A salary is a fixed annual amount paid in equal monthly instalments — common for office workers, teachers and NHS staff. It gives stable income but does not directly reward extra effort.
  • A wage is paid by the hour, often weekly. A retail assistant on £11.44 an hour (the 2024–25 UK minimum wage for those 21+) is on a wage. It rewards extra hours worked but can be unstable.
  • Commission is a percentage of sales — common in car dealerships, estate agents and at some phone retailers. It directly rewards higher selling but can push staff into hard-sell tactics.
  • Profit sharing gives staff a slice of company profits. John Lewis has historically paid an annual ‘Partnership bonus’ to all partners, though it is discretionary rather than profit-triggered — the Partnership Council chose not to pay it in 2021, 2023 and 2024 even after returning to a £56m profit. Profit sharing links individual effort to overall success and can boost teamwork, but the bonus cannot be relied on as automatic.
  • A bonus is a one-off extra payment for hitting a target — used in banking and sales.

Financial rewards matter, but only up to a point. Once pay covers basic needs, workers usually want interesting work, respect and the chance to grow. A call-centre on high basic pay with no variety still sees staff leave after six months. A research role at Dyson with a slightly lower salary but interesting projects retains people for years. This is why the specification asks you to know BOTH financial and non-financial methods — a strong business uses a mix.

Non-Financial Methods of Motivation

Non-financial methods motivate through the work itself and how it’s managed. Key approaches:

  • Styles of management. A management style shapes morale. A democratic style, where staff are consulted, builds commitment; an autocratic one, where the manager decides alone, may be fast but often demotivates.
  • Greater responsibility. Giving a worker bigger tasks, such as running a project or mentoring a junior, shows trust and develops skills. A Premier League academy coach might give a U18 assistant responsibility for match-day warm-ups — this builds confidence and loyalty.
  • Training. Investing in training tells an employee the business values them long-term. It raises skills, which raises productivity, which raises earnings. Training and motivation reinforce each other.
  • Fringe benefits. These are non-cash extras — company cars at BMW UK, free meals at Google, gym membership at PwC, private healthcare at KPMG. They make the total package more attractive without raising basic pay.

A small start-up with tight cash flow may struggle to pay big salaries but can offer shares, interesting work and a friendly culture. A large bank can pay big bonuses but also needs to invest in training and career progression to hold on to talent. The right mix depends on the budget, the type of work, the workforce and the competition. Repetitive work (picking orders in a warehouse) usually needs more financial reward; creative or skilled work (a product designer at Dyson) is often driven more by non-financial factors.

Motivation and the Wider Business

Motivation is not a standalone HR topic — it connects to operations, marketing and finance. Motivated production staff make fewer faulty products, which cuts the costs of quality control and customer complaints. Motivated sales staff speak more enthusiastically about the product, which supports the marketing effort. Motivated employees often stay when the economy dips, protecting the business during tough trading years. Each pound spent on motivation therefore has to be weighed against the gain in productivity and retention — which is why larger businesses measure staff engagement through regular surveys.

Poor motivation shows up in hard numbers. A factory with a demotivated workforce typically sees higher absenteeism (staff calling in sick), higher staff turnover and more scrap or rework. A shop with a demotivated team sees lower mystery-shopper scores and more customer complaints. These are all costs — which is why investing in motivation is not generosity, it is basic financial sense.

Key Fact

Financial methods include salary, wage, commission, profit sharing and bonuses. Non-financial methods include management style, greater responsibility, training and fringe benefits. Effective businesses combine both.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Motivational theorists such as Maslow will NOT be examined — do not waste revision time on names. You are expected to explain financial and non-financial methods and apply them to the business in the case study. In an ‘Analyse’ question, develop one method in depth (‘because… which leads to… which means…’) rather than listing five in one sentence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Motivation raises productivity and staff retention and lowers recruitment costs — it is a direct link to profit.
  • Financial methods (salary, wage, commission, profit sharing, bonus) work best for target-driven or repetitive work.
  • Non-financial methods (management style, responsibility, training, fringe benefits) work best for skilled, creative or long-service roles.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a financial method of motivation?
A) Fringe benefits
B) Greater responsibility
C) Commission

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to an estate agency of paying its sales staff on commission.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Benefit identified (e.g. staff more motivated to complete sales) + ‘because’ clause (each sale directly increases personal income) + applied to estate agency (high-value transactions mean each extra sale boosts commission noticeably, driving effort).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but generic.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named only.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A sales executive has a basic salary of £28,000 and earns 4% commission on total sales of £450,000. Calculate the executive’s total annual pay. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Commission = 0.04 × £450,000 = £18,000. Total pay = £28,000 + £18,000 = £46,000. Working shown, unit (£) included.
Secure (2 marks): Correct commission (£18,000) but arithmetic slip in the total, or correct total with missing working.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working (e.g. calculates 4% of 450,000).
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a large supermarket of introducing a profit-sharing scheme for all staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. staff feel ownership of results, which raises productivity and reduces till errors, which raises profit; however, in a year of low profit the bonus falls, which could demotivate staff and raise turnover just when the business can least afford it.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains.
Developing (1–2 marks): Listed points with little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: ‘For a call centre, paying higher wages is always the best way to motivate staff.’ Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Balanced argument with developed points both sides — e.g. higher wages do cut turnover in a repetitive job market and attract candidates; but money alone cannot fix boring tasks, poor management or lack of progression, so non-financial methods (training, responsibility, supportive management) matter too. Judgement introduces a new weighting, e.g. ‘it depends on the local labour market — in low-unemployment areas, non-financial methods are decisive; in high-unemployment areas, wages can be enough’. Not a summary.
Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present with some development, judgement offered.
Developing (4–6 marks): Mostly one-sided or listed points, limited evaluation.
Emerging (1–3 marks): Simple points, no evaluation.
No relevant content (0 marks).

lessons.title: Training
lessons.description: Induction, on-the-job and off-the-job training, and how training lifts quality.
lessons.content_html:
Training is how a business turns a willing employee into a capable one. It is not optional: roles change, technology moves and customers expect better service every year. The businesses that win are the ones whose workforce can keep up. Premier League academies, for example, run structured training programmes from U9 all the way to first-team — coaching is built into the day, not bolted on at weekends.

Why Training Matters

Training raises productivity because skilled workers complete tasks faster and with fewer mistakes. It lifts product quality and customer service, because employees know how to handle the job properly. It helps the business adapt to changes in technology — when Tesco introduced self-checkouts, staff needed retraining to help customers use them. It improves staff retention because workers who feel invested in stay longer. And it motivates staff by signalling that the business values their development.

Key Fact

Training raises productivity, quality, customer service and motivation, keeps staff in post longer and helps a business adapt to new technology.

Induction Training

Induction training is the first training a new employee receives. It introduces the business, the people, the policies and the role itself — including health and safety, fire procedures and how to log in to key systems. A new teacher at a school, for example, spends the first week meeting colleagues, walking the building, learning safeguarding rules and seeing lessons modelled.

Good induction has clear benefits. New hires settle in faster, feel welcomed and become productive more quickly. Legal risks (health and safety breaches, data mistakes) are reduced. And first impressions shape motivation: an employee whose induction was rushed or chaotic often questions whether they made the right choice.

On-the-Job Training

On-the-job training takes place in the real workplace, during normal hours. A new barista at Costa learns by shadowing an experienced one and then trying the machine while a colleague watches. In a Premier League academy, a young coach watches senior coaches run a session, then runs one under supervision.

Benefits: it is cheap (no external trainer, no travel), relevant (skills match the actual job, not a generic course) and productive (the trainee often produces useful output while learning). It is also flexible — staff can be trained in quiet periods.

Drawbacks: the trainer — the experienced colleague — is less productive while they train someone. The trainee may pick up bad habits from the trainer. And if the training is rushed, the new worker may miss important knowledge that a proper course would cover.

Off-the-Job Training

Off-the-job training happens away from the normal workplace — at a college, training centre, professional body or online. A new manager at a bank might spend a week at a leadership course. An apprentice at a construction firm might attend college one day a week. Accountancy firms send trainees to professional-body courses to pass their exams.

Benefits: expert trainers deliver specialist knowledge, there are no workplace distractions, trainees can mix with staff from other businesses and gain recognised qualifications. It is particularly useful for new technology or regulated areas like finance and law.

Drawbacks: it is more expensive (course fees, travel, lost output), less tailored to the specific workplace and the trainee produces no useful work while away. Trained staff also become more attractive to rivals — who may poach them.

Choosing the Right Method

Which method is best depends on the job, the business and the cost. Simple, practical skills (stocking shelves, pulling coffee, basic data entry) are suited to on-the-job training. Technical, regulated or specialist skills (accountancy, legal advice, new software systems) usually need off-the-job training. Many businesses use both: a retail graduate scheme at Sainsbury’s combines college-style modules with store placements. A decision in an exam question should always be justified against the specific business — a café is not a law firm.

Training and Change

Training is the main way a business handles change. When technology moves — self-checkouts at Tesco, contactless card machines at corner shops, AI tools in offices — staff who aren’t retrained are left behind. Businesses that plan training into their budget adapt faster than rivals. A John Lewis store rolling out a new stock system trains every partner before launch, which reduces mistakes on day one and means customer service holds up through the change.

Training also helps a business meet new legal or regulatory rules. When GDPR data-protection rules came in, every UK business that handled personal data had to train staff on the new requirements. Without that training, the business risked big fines from the Information Commissioner’s Office. Training is therefore not just about productivity — it is about staying on the right side of the law.

Drawbacks to Weigh

Training has drawbacks too. It costs money and takes time. Employees are less productive while being trained. Trained staff become more valuable in the wider job market, so a rival may poach them — the business has paid for training a competitor now enjoys. For small businesses with tight margins, every training decision has to be weighed carefully. This is why exam answers should never treat training as automatically ‘a good thing’; the judgement depends on cost, the likely gain and the risk of staff leaving.

Key Fact

Induction = starter training for new staff. On-the-job = learning by doing alongside a colleague. Off-the-job = learning away from the workplace at a course or college.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 9-mark ‘Justify a Decision’ questions on training, pick one method clearly and support it with two developed reasons — then weigh against the other option. Examiners reward candidates who match the method to the specific business in the case study. For Calculate questions on training cost per employee, show every step so you can earn method marks if the final number is wrong. Always include the unit (£).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Training raises productivity, quality, motivation and retention, and helps a business cope with new technology.
  • Induction training settles new staff in, on-the-job training is cheap and practical, and off-the-job training is specialist but more expensive.
  • The right mix depends on the job, the sector and the budget — always justify a choice against the specific business.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of off-the-job training?
A) A new waiter watching a senior colleague take an order
B) A barista practising on the coffee machine during a quiet shift
C) An apprentice attending college one day a week
D) A new employee being shown the fire exits on their first day
practice_questions.marks:
C) An apprentice attending college one day a week [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct answer selected.
Emerging: Incorrect answer.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘induction training’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2 marks): Clear definition — training given to new employees when they start, covering the business, their role and essential procedures.
Secure (1 mark): Basic idea (e.g. ‘training for new employees’) without precise detail.
Emerging (0 marks): Confuses induction with general training or with on-the-job training.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a Premier League academy of using on-the-job training for young coaches.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Benefit identified (e.g. skills learned are directly relevant) + ‘because’ clause (new coaches practise on the same pitches and players they will manage) + applied to academy (means coaching style stays consistent with the club’s philosophy).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but generic.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named only.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A business sends 8 employees on an off-the-job training course. The course costs £450 per employee and each employee loses 2 days of output worth £160 per day. Calculate the total cost to the business of the training. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Course cost = 8 × £450 = £3,600. Lost output = 8 × 2 × £160 = £2,560. Total = £6,160. Working shown, unit (£) included.
Secure (2 marks): One subtotal correct but error in the other, or correct total without working.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working (e.g. spots 8 × £450).
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a large supermarket of the introduction of self-service checkouts and the training needed to support them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. retraining staff to help customers with self-checkouts speeds up queues and raises customer service, which boosts loyalty; however, training time is expensive and older staff may resist the change, leading to short-term productivity losses before gains appear.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains.
Developing (1–2 marks): Listed points with little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: A growing bakery with 20 staff needs to train new assistants. The owner is choosing between on-the-job training led by existing bakers, or sending new assistants on a one-week off-the-job course at a local college. Justify which method the owner should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9 marks): Two developed reasons for the chosen option (one fully explained) — e.g. on-the-job is cheaper for a small bakery, keeps staff available to serve customers, and trainees learn the house recipes exactly. Weighed against counter (college course offers food-hygiene qualification, reduces the load on senior bakers). Clear judgement matched to the specific bakery.
Secure (4–6 marks): Some development of both options. Judgement present but brief.
Developing (1–3 marks): Mainly listing pros and cons.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.
